title: IMGNN: An Efficient, Effective and Generalizable Algorithm for Influence Maximization in Social Networks

problem.claim: Influence maximization in social networks seeks to identify seed nodes that maximize influence spread.

gap.claim: Traditional influence-maximization methods lack generalizability and require an explicitly defined influence diffusion model, while learning-based methods have severe scalability and generalizability deficiencies.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes IMGNN, a graph-neural-network-based learning algorithm for influence maximization designed for efficiency, effectiveness, and generalizability.

IMGNN constructs features from influence propagations over graphs with randomly skipped nodes and trains on smaller networks to improve time efficiency and reduce overfitting to specific network structures.
IMGNN supports training on small-scale graphs followed by direct seed-node-set inference on large-scale graphs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the feature-construction and model-training design based on influence propagations over graphs with randomly skipped nodes as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report better efficiency and effectiveness than existing influence-maximization algorithms.
The authors report extensive experiments on real-world social networks with up to 40 million nodes.
The authors report superiority in influence spread, seed-node-set inference speed, and generalizability.

narrative_sequence.summary: Influence maximization is an important and extensively studied social-network-analysis problem.
Traditional and learning-based approaches are limited by dependence on diffusion-model definitions, weak generalizability, and poor scalability.
The paper introduces IMGNN, a graph-neural-network-based algorithm intended to improve efficiency, effectiveness, and generalizability.
IMGNN uses randomly skipped-node influence-propagation features and smaller-network training to reduce structural overfitting and improve time efficiency.
Experiments on real-world social networks of up to 40 million nodes are reported to show superior influence spread, inference speed, and generalizability.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact model architecture, training objective, diffusion assumptions, or baseline configurations.
The abstract does not provide quantitative experimental results, datasets, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not establish independent verification or reproducibility.
